walkthroughs.body_html:
Forces & Motion — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Forces & Motion brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Forces & Motion.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A car travels 4 km north then 3 km east. What is its displacement magnitude?
options: 7 km
5 km
1 km
25 km

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
options: Acceleration
Momentum
Kinetic energy
Weight

mcqs.q: If an object is moving at constant velocity in a straight line, what is the net force on it?
options: Zero — by Newton's first law, constant velocity requires zero net force.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
There must be a forward force on the object to keep it moving.
The net force equals the velocity times the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: When you push a wall, what does Newton's third law say about the wall?
options: The wall only pushes back if your force is strong enough to make it react.
The wall exerts an equal and opposite force on you at the same instant.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
Mass changes with location but weight does not.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
options: Mass changes with location but weight does not.
The wall pushes back with a force proportional to how stiff it is, not equal to your force.
Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on that mass (N) and depends on g.
Mass and weight are the same thing, just expressed in different units.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Resolving vectors”?
options: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Vector”?
options: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Velocity”?
options: Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with both magnitude and direction, such as velocity, force, or displacement.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Displacement”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Scalar”?
options: Rate of change of displacement with respect to time, measured in m s⁻¹.
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Acceleration”?
options: Splitting a vector into perpendicular components, typically using F cos θ and F sin θ.
The vector from an initial to a final position; the straight-line change in position.
Rate of change of velocity with respect to time, measured in m s⁻².
A quantity with magnitude only, such as mass, time, speed, or energy.
